value.0: You know the rule of my counter by now: if you're standing there, you're holding something. Here - keep that level while I titrate. The sublevel drains clean these days, the wards upstairs got their kolto pressure back, and the only person building an emergency cocktail below Dantooine is you, when someone's dying and the minutes run short. That's how it should be. I even slept last week. Don't spread that around.

Careful - don't touch that rack. Your reach says confidence, but your hands say first aid isn't finished with you yet. The craft has layers under the ones you've learned, and I only teach the last one. Wring everything out of the wards first - every technique, every hour they'll give you. When there's nothing left up there to learn, come back to my counter. I'll still be awake.

Hold this vial - level, don't tilt it, it's mid-titration and I don't own a spare. Good. You have working hands, so listen. There's a crew in the sublevel under this facility running my discipline backwards: hot stabilizer batches, mixed fast, tested on patients who can't crawl off the cot. Their adepts hold the arms down. Put six of them down instead, and bring me the book they log the doses in - the Emergency Cocktail Triage Ward Ledger. My format, their handwriting. I want it off their counter and onto mine.

Take the key off that hook - the one with the red tag. It opens the sealed hatch down past the supply lifts, into the Dantooine Medical Sublevel. Six adepts, one ledger, and don't drink anything you find in an unmarked flask. Minutes matter more the longer you stand here.

A stabilizer you build under fire. No clean bench, no scale, no second try - just what's in your kit and a patient losing the argument with their own blood pressure. Done right, it buys minutes that don't exist. Done the way that crew does it, it's a coin flip with someone else's heart. That's the difference you're going down there to enforce.

Under your feet. This facility sits on a sublevel from the old enclave days - kolto conduits, triage rooms, storage nobody audited in a decade. That's the Dantooine Medical Sublevel. The entry hatch is sealed; the key I keep on that hook opens it. Past the supply lifts, down the service stairs, follow the pipe markings. Everything below the hatch is theirs, not ours. For now.

Chemists who stopped asking permission. The adepts are dosed on their own product - faster than they should be, numb where you'd hope they weren't. They'll come at you with scalpels and injectors, and if one grabs you, count your pulse, because whatever's in the syringe works in seconds. Keep your kit stocked and your exits counted.
The ledger's still down there, and so are the six adepts writing in it. Every hour you spend up here, that book gains a page. Go.
That smell - antiseptic and scorched sugar. You found their counter. Hand the ledger over before I say something grateful.

Forty doses in nine days, initialed like it's something to be proud of. Six sets of initials that won't appear again, thanks to you. Credits are in the drawer - hazard rate, because I'm not insulting either of us. When your hands have recovered, come back. The next lesson costs more.

You again. Good - hold this coupler housing while I talk, it wants a steady grip. The crew took the ledger loss badly. Their specialists have spliced feed lines straight into the sublevel's kolto conduits: raw kolto into hot batches, no filtration, straight into whoever's strapped down. Five specialists run the splice. Take them apart and bring me the fitting itself - the Emergency Cocktail Kolto Conduit Coupler. Without it their whole draw collapses, and I get proof of exactly what they tapped.

Same hatch, same key. Cut the specialists away from the conduit junctions before they can vent anything at you, and bring the coupler back intact. A cracked one tells me nothing except that you were careless.

An adept holds the arm. A specialist decides what goes into it. They trained under real ward staff before they went below, which means they know dosage, timing, and precisely how much a body can take before it stops complaining. They will use all three on you.

Because a splice fitting is a signature. The coupler will show the machining, the batch residue, the draw rate - enough for me to prove to this facility's board that its own kolto lines fed the operation. The ledger told me what they did. The coupler tells me what it cost the wards upstairs.

Rougher than last time. The specialists work in pairs and they don't panic - panic is for people who haven't already decided you're a test subject. Watch the conduit valves; they'll vent kolto steam to blind you, and what comes through the cloud isn't medicine. Go in rested. That's a prescription, not a suggestion.
Five specialists, one coupler, and a kolto line bleeding into bad batches the whole time you're up here. The math doesn't pause. Neither should you.
You're carrying something heavy and machined, and your jacket smells like kolto steam. That's my coupler. Counter. Now.

Look at this draw gauge - they were pulling triple what a ward pulls in a full emergency, around the clock. This goes to the board with my compliments and your fingerprints wiped off. Credits in the drawer. You're becoming a line item in my budget, which is the closest thing to affection I keep in stock.

Put the tray down and listen, because this one changes the dosage. Past the conduit junctions there's a sealed ward - the crew's clean room, where the real batches get made. The door answers to one person: their warden. Ward-trained, dosed to the eyes, and big enough that the specialists knock. I want the warden gone and their mark pried off that door - the Emergency Cocktail Fractured Ward Sigil comes back to me. And you don't go down alone. That's triage math, not sentiment: one of you bleeds out in that room. Three of you walk out. Bring two people you'd trust with your airway.

Good answer - the plural was the part I was checking. The clean room is past the junction rooms, behind the door wearing the cracked sigil. Hit the warden fast, keep someone breathing between injectors, and pry the sigil loose when it's done. I'll have three stims and a strong opinion waiting.

She ran a trauma ward upstairs for six years. Best hands I ever watched work - and then she decided consent was a bottleneck. Now she guards their mixing room and doses herself from the stock. Whatever speed and strength you're imagining, add more, and remember she knows exactly where you keep your arteries. Professionally.

Simple sums. One fighter in that room means the warden picks when you rest, when you bleed, and when it ends. Two means someone can drag the other clear. Three means she has to choose, and choosing is where fights get lost. I've run this arithmetic on cot after cot for twenty years. Bring two companions, or don't bring yourself.

It marked that room as a protected ward - my predecessor's mark, from when the sublevel still healed people. The crew cracked it when they took the room, then left it hanging on the door like a joke. Bring me the fractured half. I'd rather it sit broken in my drawer than whole on their door.
The warden's still holding that door, and if you're standing here alone, you're still two people short of a survivable entry. Gather your trusted pair, then go take that sigil off her door.
You're moving like someone who got hit hard and treated fast - which means your companions did their jobs. Is that the sigil? Give it here.

There's the crack, right through the ward mark. They wanted the joke on record; now it's evidence. The clean room's dark, the warden's off the board, and this facility owes you more than what's in my drawer - but the drawer is what I control, so take it. And tell your two they have standing credit at my counter. That's not nothing.

Sit. I already poured you a stimulant - that's how you know it's serious. With the warden gone, the crew's core came up from the deep rooms. Four of them. The inner circle, the ones who wrote the hot-batch doctrine in the first place. They've taken the old matron's ward - the last part of the sublevel that was still sacred - and they're holding the Emergency Cocktail Matron's Ward Token, her own mark of care, pocketed like a trophy. Four names, one token. Bring it back and the sublevel's history stops being theirs to spend.

The matron's ward is the deepest room before the master's own. They'll be together - the circle doesn't split. That's their strength and their vanity, so break the vanity. Keep your companions close; four trained sets of hands against one of yours is arithmetic I've already given you my opinion on.

The founders. Two washed out of this facility's certification board, one mixed for a mercenary column, and the fourth - the fourth trained me, years ago, which is a sentence I'd rather you forgot. They built the doctrine the adepts died practicing. Every dose in that ledger traces uphill to those four signatures.

Before this was a facility, it was one ward run by one matron, back when the enclave conduits still hummed. Her token passed hand to hand; whoever held it answered for every patient below. The circle took it because holding it says the sublevel answers to them. I don't run on sentiment, but I make an exception for that piece of brass.

Four practitioners who've each survived their own doctrine, in a room with one door. They'll stagger their injectors so one is always fresh while three circle you. If your two from the warden's door are still upright, this is where you spend that trust again. Overlap your minutes. Don't trade one-for-one with people who keep spares.
The circle is still holding the matron's ward, and the token is still in the wrong pocket. Four names. I've crossed out none of them yet.
Your hands are steadier than mine tonight, and that's a first for this counter. Show me the token.

Brass, and lighter than its job description. Four signatures closed out, and the ward they were squatting in goes back to being a ward. I'd call that a good shift, and I haven't called anything a good shift in two years. Credits in the drawer. Rest and restock - the deep room is still lit, and we both know who's in it.

No tray this time. Both hands free, because you should hear this straight. The one left below is the master - the chemist the circle answered to. He finished what I never dared: the emergency cocktail, perfected. He can stand in a collapsing ward, build a stabilizer from pocket vials, and pull himself back from the edge mid-fight, over and over. It cost a wing full of patients to refine, and he'd tell you it was worth it. Kill him, and the recipe stops being his - then it's yours, built clean, the way I'll teach it. And hear the dosage on this part: taken alone, the master's room is a lethal dose. Every time. Nobody. Take your two, or take more.

Then this is the last thing I hand you: every stim I've mixed this month. Split them among your companions. The deep room is past the matron's ward, and he'll know you're coming - he's been reading the same ledger entries backwards. When he goes down, don't collect anything. Walk back up breathing. That's the only proof I need.

An entire recovery wing. Twenty-six beds. He needed subjects at the exact edge of death to tune the timing, so he manufactured the edge. The cocktail works - that's the unbearable part. Every one of those patients stabilized beautifully, right up until he needed the bed for the next iteration. Perfection with a body count. That's what you're ending.

Because I already tried. Years ago, when it was him and me and one shared bench. I ran, he stayed, and everything below that hatch is what staying looks like. My hands still mix a fair cocktail, but they shake when that door comes up in conversation, and shaking hands kill patients. You're my steady hands now. That's the whole confession - don't make me repeat it.

Like a man who has never once worried about dying, because for him it's a solved problem. He'll take wounds that should end it, drink his own work, and stand back up with his pulse reset. You can't out-wait him alone and you can't out-bleed him alone. Three of you, rotating, wearing him down between doses - the recipe has a seam, and the seam is minutes. Spend yours better than he spends his.
The deep room is still lit. Take your people, take the stims, and go put the recipe out of his hands. I'll be awake. I'm always awake.
You came up those stairs slow, and you're not carrying anything - which, this one time, is exactly right. Tell me it's done.

Then sit down, because class starts now. The emergency cocktail, built clean - no strapped-down subjects, no forced doses, no ledger. Just your kit, your minutes, and hands I've watched earn this one stage at a time. He perfected it on other people's blood; you'll carry it on your own. That distinction is the entire discipline. The drawer's open - take the credits, then take a stool. First lesson: nothing you build under fire is ever for you.
Back to the job.
Give me the way down. I'll get your ledger.
What is an emergency cocktail, exactly?
How do I reach this sublevel?
What's waiting for me down there?
Not today. Find another set of hands.
Their Triage Ward Ledger. Every dose is in it.
Back to the specialists.
Five specialists. I'll bring you the coupler.
What makes a specialist worse than an adept?
Why does the coupler matter so much?
How rough will it get down there this time?
My kit's empty. I'll come back restocked.
One Kolto Conduit Coupler, mostly intact.
Back to the warden.
I'll find two I trust and put the warden down.
Who is this warden?
Walk me through your triage math.
What's the ward sigil to you?
Not until I have the right people beside me.
The Fractured Ward Sigil, off the clean room door.
Back to the circle.
Four of them, one token. Done.
Who are these four?
What's the matron's token to the sublevel?
Four at once. What am I walking into?
Let me settle my nerves first.
The Matron's Ward Token. The circle is finished.
Back to the master.
We go down together, and I'll finish it.
What did perfecting it cost him?
Why haven't you gone down there yourself?
How does he fight?
Not yet. This one deserves my best.
He's dead. The recipe is ours now.
